title: When a WordPress plugin is the right tool
summary: A practical way to decide whether a feature belongs in a plugin, theme, or existing service.

sections.heading: Start with the job
sections.body: Define what the feature needs to do, who uses it, and which data it touches. That answer matters more than the initial implementation choice.

sections.heading: Keep business logic portable
sections.body: A plugin can keep custom behavior independent from a theme. That is useful when the design changes but the workflow must remain.

sections.heading: Check the maintenance cost
sections.body: Use an existing plugin when its behavior and support fit the job. Build custom code when the workflow is specific enough that general-purpose settings become a burden.

title: When a static site makes sense
summary: Static-first is a useful default for content that rarely needs server-side work.

sections.heading: Match the architecture to the work
sections.body: A portfolio or focused marketing site usually needs fast pages, clear content, and a dependable inquiry path. It may not need a complex runtime.

sections.heading: Keep dynamic features deliberate
sections.body: Forms, search, and private accounts can still be added where required. The point is to avoid loading the whole site with client-side code for a small feature.

title: SEO foundations before launch
summary: A checklist for making a small business site understandable to visitors and search engines.

sections.heading: Give every page a purpose
sections.body: Use a descriptive page title, a specific heading, and content that answers the visitor's question.

sections.heading: Make the technical basics reliable
sections.body: Check indexing, canonical URLs, sitemap links, accessible navigation, and image descriptions before discussing advanced tactics.

title: What to check before choosing website hosting
summary: A hosting decision is about maintenance and recovery as much as speed.

sections.heading: Define the support model
sections.body: Know who handles updates, backups, incidents, and restore tests. A low monthly price does not answer those questions.

sections.heading: Measure the live site
sections.body: Use monitoring and performance checks after launch. Avoid promising an uptime figure that has not been measured.

title: How I run a website project with clients
summary: Clear scope and quick feedback make the build easier for both sides.

sections.heading: Start with the business task
sections.body: We define the audience, desired action, and content you can provide before choosing a visual direction.

sections.heading: Build in review points
sections.body: Early structure and copy reviews reduce expensive changes near launch. After testing, I hand over a site the owner can maintain.

title: Design for the next useful action
summary: Good hierarchy helps a visitor understand the offer and decide what to do.

sections.heading: Make the offer easy to scan
sections.body: Lead with a concrete promise and support it with relevant work. Avoid asking visitors to decode internal language.

sections.heading: Put proof near the decision
sections.body: Show actual work, explain your role, and make the next step obvious. Never substitute invented numbers for evidence.
